newsitem.title: ITALY: Turkey told to take steps against money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Turkey told to take steps against money laundering.

text.p: Turkey must introduce laws to fight money laundering or else face potentially damaging action by the world's banking community, the international Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned on Thursday.
The 26-nation group said in a report released after a meeting in Rome that Turkey was the only FATF member not to have satisfied organisation rules on money laundering legislation.
If it did not move swiftly, the FATF said it would instruct banks in member countries to pay particular attention to all business relations and transactions with Turkey.

"Their banking system will suffer badly if all major countries start carefully scrutinising their deals," said Stanely Morris, a FATF member and a director of the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
FATF officials said if the recommendation came into force, it could cause long delays for delivery of Turkish exports and imports while the origins of the funds were checked.

FATF was set up in 1989 by the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialised nations to combat the growing problem of money laundering, which is estimated to involve anywhere between $300-600 billion a year.

Last year the group introduced a 40-point battle plan, including the extension of money laundering crimes beyond drug trafficking and requiring mandatory reporting of suspicious transactions by financial institutions.
"But we can't go out and tell everyone else what to do when one of our own members hasn't done so," FATF chairman Fernando Carpentieri told a news conference, referring to Turkey.
He said if the necessary laws were not introduced by September, FATF would send a task force to Ankara to discuss the situation, after which regulatory action would be taken.
Turkey has already drawn up legislation to outlaw formally the laundering of illegally earned money, but Carpentieri said it had not been enacted because of recent political turmoil.
"While we sympathise with this...we do not think it is an acceptable excuse," he said. Turkish officials at the meeting were not available for comment.
Italian police believe a growing amount of hard drugs are being smuggled into Europe via Turkey. "There is a huge potential from money laundering in Turkey," Morris said.

The only other time the FATF has ordered bank controls on a country was against non-member Seychelles in 1995 when it presented legislation granting asset protection and legal immunity to individuals who invested there.
"They suspended the law almost immediately," Morris said.
When the FATF was set up, only Britain and the United States had anti-money laundering statutes. Now 25 countries do and some 60 other countries have made commitments to follow suit.

But officials said simply having legislation did not mean an end to money laundering operations and FATF is believed to be unhappy about prevention measures in a number of member countries, including the United States and Austria.
A FATF official said a full annual report due to be released shortly "would include some firm language" about this.
He said there was particular concern about the increasing use of bureaux de change and non-bank financial institutions to hide money laundering activities.
